species.name: Asian koel
species.habitat: Fruiting trees in parks and woodland
species.rarity: Common; often heard rather than seen
species.fact: A koel chick can be raised by a crow after its egg was laid in the crow’s nest.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2016
species.summary: The loud morning caller many Singapore residents know by sound. It is a cuckoo whose chicks are raised in another bird’s nest.
species.identification: Males are glossy black with a pale bill and red eyes. Females are brown with pale spots and bars, so the two sexes look quite different.
species.diet: Mainly fruit, with other food taken opportunistically.
species.activity: Diurnal; calling can begin early in the morning.
species.behaviour: Often stays in foliage around fruiting trees. Its repeated call is more conspicuous than the bird itself.
species.reproduction: Lays eggs in other birds’ nests, including crows’ nests. The host adults provide the chick’s care: this is called brood parasitism.
species.singapore: Common in secondary woodland, gardens, parks and other urban greenery. It is a native resident, not an introduced noise-making species.
species.ecologicalRole: A fruit consumer and brood parasite in the local bird community.
species.pressures: Loss of fruiting trees removes food. Managing noise complaints should not involve disturbing wildlife nests.
species.watch: Listen from a distance and avoid playback. Do not search for or interfere with a host nest.

species.name: Asian leaf turtle
species.habitat: Forest streams
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: The hatchling has a flattened shell densely patterned with dark spots; adults have a dark-brown shell.
species.summary: A secretive stream-associated turtle, listed as Critically Endangered in Singapore. Its subdued colours fit the shaded forest setting.
species.identification: An oval, dark-brown shell with a toothed rear edge; orange lines mark the dark head and neck. Hatchlings are flatter and more densely spotted than adults.
species.diet: An omnivore that eats both plant and animal material.
species.activity: NParks describes apparent nocturnal activity; detailed Singapore activity patterns remain poorly documented.
species.behaviour: Associated with forest streams and their banks. Limited sightings make this an animal to learn about without seeking out sensitive sites.
species.reproduction: Lays eggs; local nesting timing and clutch sizes have not been verified.
species.singapore: NParks documents catchment-forest records from 2006 and 2007. These are historical observations, while RDB3 (2024) retains the species as nationally Critically Endangered; neither is a current population census.
species.ecologicalRole: Its mixed diet connects plant material and animal prey within the forest-stream food web.
species.pressures: Habitat degradation and collection for food or trade are identified threats. Forest streams and surrounding cover need protection.
species.watch: Stay out of streams and leave turtles, eggs and cover undisturbed. Do not collect or release pet turtles into natural habitats.

species.name: Banded bullfrog
species.habitat: Gardens, built areas and temporary pools
species.fact: A threatened bullfrog can inflate its body to appear larger.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A round-bodied frog often heard after rain in Singapore. It adapts well to gardens and built areas but is recorded by NParks as introduced here.
species.identification: A small head, rounded body and two broad pale bands against a darker back. It can inflate its body when threatened.
species.diet: Ants, termites and other small invertebrates.
species.activity: Mostly nocturnal; calling often follows rain.
species.behaviour: Shelters in covered places and can climb as well as move on the ground. Its low call may carry farther than expected from its size.
species.reproduction: Gathers near temporary pools or other still water to breed. Eggs develop into aquatic tadpoles before metamorphosis into frogs.
species.singapore: Common in gardens, parks and other built environments. Being well established is different from being native.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes small invertebrates and is itself prey for other animals.
species.pressures: Traffic and loss of usable breeding water affect encounters locally. Do not introduce frogs or tadpoles to new sites.
species.watch: Listen after rain from a safe path. Leave adults, eggs and tadpoles in place.

species.name: Black-eyed litter frog
species.habitat: Forest floor and streams
species.rarity: Elusive; common within some forest habitat
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Researchers identify its rapid, rattling call even when the frog itself stays hidden.
species.summary: A small leaf-litter frog with conspicuous dark eyes and a surprisingly distinctive voice. Being common within a forest patch does not mean it is widespread across Singapore.
species.identification: Large head and black eyes, relatively short slender limbs, and grey or brown skin marked with irregular dark patches. The pale underside has dark speckling.
species.diet: Insectivorous, feeding on small animal prey in its forest-floor habitat.
species.activity: Mainly nocturnal.
species.behaviour: Lives among fallen leaves. Its rapid rattling call can be easier to notice than its camouflaged body.
species.reproduction: Has an aquatic tadpole stage. NParks describes the larvae as large and almost black; no verified Singapore clutch-size or fixed breeding-season estimate is supplied here.
species.singapore: Associated with the Central Nature Reserves and forest stream habitats. NParks surveys found it frequently in suitable forest, while RDB3 assesses it as nationally Near Threatened.
species.ecologicalRole: An insect predator within the forest-floor food web, with aquatic larvae linking the life cycle to water.
species.pressures: Maintaining connected, moist forest and its water habitats is important for this habitat-associated frog; local frequency should not be confused with habitat security.
species.watch: Observe without moving logs or leaves. Keep out of streams, avoid playback and flash, and leave amphibians and tadpoles untouched.

species.name: Black-naped oriole
species.habitat: Tree canopies in parks, gardens and woodland
species.fact: Its Malay name, ‘kunyit besar’, refers to the bird’s striking yellow colour.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2018
species.summary: A bright yellow bird of Singapore’s tree canopy. Its distinctive colour can stand out in flight but disappear surprisingly well among sunlit leaves.
species.identification: Yellow body, black wings and a broad dark eye band continuing around the back of the head. Adults have a pinkish bill; young birds have streakier underparts.
species.diet: Fruit and insects.
species.activity: Diurnal.
species.behaviour: Forages in trees and may join other birds at fruiting plants. Look high in the foliage and listen as well as watch.
species.reproduction: Builds a cup-like nest suspended in a fork of branches. Eggs and young stay protected within the nest.
species.singapore: Widespread in parks, gardens and other wooded settings. It is listed as native and nationally Least Concern.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes fruit and insects in the canopy food web.
species.pressures: Retention of mature trees and food plants supports nesting and foraging.
species.watch: Watch feeding birds from the path. Avoid pointing out or approaching active nests.

species.name: Blue-eared kingfisher
species.habitat: Shaded forest streams and mangroves
species.rarity: Uncommon resident of wooded water margins
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Its nest is reached through a tunnel it digs into a stream bank.
species.summary: A small resident kingfisher of shaded waterways. Its strong blue-and-rust colours can disappear surprisingly well against dark water and forest cover.
species.identification: Around 16 cm long, with deep cobalt-blue upperparts and rich rusty underparts. Adult males have dark bills; females can show red on the lower bill or more extensively. It is smaller and darker blue than the Common Kingfisher.
species.diet: Small fish and aquatic invertebrates caught around sheltered water.
species.activity: Look for daytime perch-and-dive hunting beside shaded water; a full local daily activity pattern is not quantified here.
species.behaviour: May bob its head and flick its tail while watching from a perch. After a dive, it can beat captured prey against a branch before swallowing.
species.reproduction: Excavates a nesting tunnel in a forest-stream bank. This guide omits exact nest positions and does not extrapolate overseas clutch sizes or breeding months to Singapore.
species.singapore: Bird Society of Singapore lists it as an uncommon resident that favours dense woodland and mangroves. NParks has also documented use of the Eco-Link@BKE wildlife bridge; the bridge is not a public viewing site.
species.ecologicalRole: A small predator linking stream invertebrates and fish to the surrounding wooded food web.
species.pressures: Maintaining shaded waterways and undisturbed banks follows from its documented feeding and nesting needs. This is a habitat-based conservation recommendation, not a quantified local decline claim.
species.watch: Remain on public paths and give bank vegetation space. Do not clear branches for photographs, bait the bird, play calls or approach a burrow entrance.

species.name: Buffy fish owl
species.habitat: Forested waterways and mangroves
species.rarity: Uncommon resident; often hidden by day
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: The pointed tufts on its head are feather ornaments, not exposed ears.
species.summary: A large owl adapted to hunting beside water. Singapore has a resident population, but daytime resting and night activity can make individual birds difficult to notice.
species.identification: Look for yellow eyes, outward-pointing feather tufts and warm brown plumage with dark streaks. The tufts are not its actual ears. Bird Society of Singapore gives an adult length of about 46–47 cm.
species.diet: Fish, crabs and frogs, with other small prey such as rats taken around banks.
species.activity: Mostly nocturnal; rests among tree foliage during the day.
species.behaviour: Often watches water from a low branch before swooping for prey. Its unfeathered lower legs and gripping feet suit this fishing lifestyle.
species.reproduction: A documented Singapore nesting observation found a chick in a bird's-nest fern in 2016. Such records establish local breeding, but do not provide a complete island-wide breeding calendar.
species.singapore: Associated with wooded streams, reservoirs and mangroves. NParks records it in the Central Catchment and Pulau Ubin; these are broad occurrence areas, not nest directions or guaranteed sightings.
species.ecologicalRole: Its diet links aquatic prey and land animals to a nocturnal predator in the same wetland food web.
species.pressures: NParks identifies illegal trapping as a threat. Keeping suitable trees and quiet water margins is a habitat-based conservation priority, not a measured population trend.
species.watch: Watch from open paths using binoculars. Avoid flash, prolonged torchlight, playback or crowding a resting bird. Never approach a nest or publish its precise position.

funFacts.text: The pointed tufts on its head are feather ornaments, not exposed ears.

funFacts.title: An owl with audible wings
funFacts.text: Its flight is less silent than that of many other owls: fish owls lack the same degree of sound-muffling feather specialisation.

species.name: Changeable hawk-eagle
species.habitat: Forest, woodland and wooded edges
species.rarity: Resident; may be seen or heard near woodland
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2020
species.fact: Pale and dark hawk-eagles can belong to the same species; these colour forms are called morphs.
species.globalAssessmentNote: Published assessment: 2020, cited by The Peregrine Fund. The exact assessment date was not recovered; this is a dated reference, not a claim of the latest assessment.
species.summary: A resident forest raptor whose plumage can look dramatically different between individuals. It can be conspicuous above woodland while still depending on places to hunt and nest.
species.identification: Adults occur in pale and dark colour forms. Pale adults have streaked light underparts; dark adults are largely dark brown. Pale juveniles can show much cleaner white underparts. Its length is about 61–75 cm, so colour alone is insufficient for identification.
species.diet: Birds, small mammals and reptiles such as snakes and lizards; it may occasionally scavenge.
species.activity: Diurnal; hunts, perches and soars during the day.
species.behaviour: Often hunts by waiting quietly on a concealed perch, then making a short attack when prey comes within reach. It may also soar above wooded areas.
species.reproduction: Both partners construct a stick nest in a tall tree, lining it with greenery. Species accounts describe a single egg and prolonged care; breeding dates differ across its range and are not a Singapore schedule.
species.singapore: NParks records it in forest reserves and Pulau Ubin and highlights it in woodland birdwatching at Kranji Marshes. Bird Society lists it as a common resident; frequency of observation does not remove its national Vulnerable status.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of several animal groups that links different parts of the woodland food web.
species.pressures: The Peregrine Fund identifies habitat loss, fragmentation and persecution across the species' range. These are range-wide pressures, not a measured Singapore population trend.
species.watch: Scan the canopy from public trails. Never bait a raptor or approach an occupied nest. Keep the bird's flight path clear and watch through binoculars.

funFacts.title: One species, two looks
funFacts.text: Pale and dark hawk-eagles can belong to the same species; these colour forms are called morphs.

funFacts.title: A nest-building team
funFacts.text: Both members of a pair help build their large stick nest and finish it with green leaves.

species.name: Clouded monitor
species.habitat: Forest and wooded parks
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Nostril position helps tell the two common monitors apart: the clouded monitor's nostril sits farther back from the snout tip.
species.summary: A native monitor that is as comfortable climbing trees as exploring the forest floor. It generally favours land habitats more than the familiar water monitor.
species.identification: Brown with yellow spotting. Compared with a Malayan water monitor, the head is shorter, the tail more rounded and the nostril sits farther back, about midway between the eye and snout tip. Use several features together.
species.diet: Searches through leaf litter for worms and other invertebrates.
species.activity: Diurnal: active during daylight, as documented in local forest surveys.
species.behaviour: Forages on the ground and climbs trees. Its ability to use both levels is a useful reminder to look above ground as well as along paths.
species.reproduction: Lays eggs. Local nesting dates, clutch size and incubation periods are not asserted from unrelated captive accounts.
species.singapore: NParks describes it as relatively common in suitable habitats, including forest and wooded gardens. This does not mean it is equally frequent in every neighbourhood.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of small ground-dwelling animals within the leaf-litter food web.
species.pressures: Retaining forest cover, leaf litter and climbing trees helps preserve its habitat. Its local Least Concern label does not remove the need for respectful encounters.
species.watch: Watch from a distance and allow it to pass. Never feed, corner or handle a monitor, and keep pets under control.

species.name: Collared kingfisher
species.habitat: Mangroves, coasts, canals and parks
species.fact: Its menu includes lizards and insects, so it can live away from water.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2024
species.summary: A familiar kingfisher that is not limited to fishing. It watches from a perch and can hunt small land animals well away from water.
species.identification: Blue-green upperparts with a white collar and belly. The large bill is dark, unlike the red bill of a white-throated kingfisher.
species.diet: Fish, small amphibians, lizards and insects.
species.activity: Diurnal.
species.behaviour: Hunts from fences, wires and exposed branches. Usually territorial outside the breeding period.
species.reproduction: Nests in a cavity or burrow. Do not inspect an opening or approach birds repeatedly carrying food to it.
species.singapore: Common along coasts and canals and in parks, including suitable mangrove habitats. NParks describes it as the most common local kingfisher.
species.ecologicalRole: A small predator using both terrestrial and waterside food webs.
species.pressures: Loss of vegetation, perches and nesting cover reduces useful habitat.
species.watch: Use binoculars from a fixed point. Let the bird resume hunting rather than following it between perches.

species.name: Common house gecko
species.habitat: Buildings, gardens and nearby woodland
species.fact: A gecko can shed its tail to distract a threat, but the replacement is not identical.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A small night-active lizard familiar on walls and near lights. Several gecko species use Singapore’s buildings, so a distant outline is not enough for a certain identification.
species.identification: Expanded toe pads, thin skin and small spines around an original tail. A regrown tail can look different, so tail shape alone is not conclusive.
species.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates.
species.activity: Nocturnal; shelters in cracks by day.
species.behaviour: Climbs walls and trees to hunt. It may shed its tail when threatened, giving it a chance to escape.
species.reproduction: Females usually lay two small, hard-shelled eggs in protected places. Hatchlings are miniature lizards, without a tadpole stage.
species.singapore: Common in buildings and nearby wooded areas. It is listed in Singapore’s national reptile assessment as Least Concern.
species.ecologicalRole: A small insect predator around buildings and vegetation.
species.pressures: Sticky traps and pesticides can harm geckos and their prey.
species.watch: Do not catch it by the tail. Avoid glue traps and let it move away normally.

funFacts.text: A gecko can shed its tail to distract a threat, but the replacement is not identical.

species.name: Dugong
species.habitat: Coastal seas, estuaries and seagrass beds
species.rarity: Rarely seen in Singapore waters; no population estimate implied
species.summary: A marine mammal that grazes on seagrass. Singapore records link this quiet swimmer to shallow coastal waters and river mouths.
species.identification: A bulky grey-brown body, blunt bristled muzzle, paired front flippers and a fluked tail. It has no dorsal fin.
species.diet: Mainly seagrass, gathered from underwater meadows.
species.activity: Feeding and resting alternate; the local NParks account describes night feeding and daytime rest in deeper water.
species.behaviour: May travel alone, with another dugong or in small groups. It surfaces to breathe and remains fully aquatic.
species.reproduction: A female normally produces one calf after a pregnancy lasting about thirteen to fourteen months. She nurses the calf. These general life-history notes do not establish a Singapore breeding season.
species.singapore: NParks records it mainly from the north-eastern Johor Straits. Records also include Changi, Pulau Ubin, Pulau Tekong and Labrador. A recorded location does not guarantee a sighting.
species.ecologicalRole: Seagrass feeding connects coastal vegetation with the marine food web.
species.pressures: Boat propellers, fishing-net entanglement, water pollution and loss of seagrass feeding grounds threaten dugongs.
species.watch: Observe from shore where possible. Never chase, feed or approach an animal with a boat. Report a stranded animal to NParks or ACRES and follow their instructions.
species.fact: A dugong has no dorsal fin.

funFacts.title: A smooth back
funFacts.text: Unlike a dolphin, a dugong has no dorsal fin.

funFacts.title: An underwater grazer
funFacts.text: Its food meadow grows beneath the sea: dugongs feed on seagrass.

species.taxonomyNote: A sirenian mammal, not a dolphin or a fish. Similar swimming shapes do not imply close ancestry.

species.name: Equatorial spitting cobra
species.habitat: Scrub, forest edges and suburban greenery
species.fact: A hood and hiss are defensive warnings, not an invitation to move closer.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A venomous native snake that sometimes enters built areas. Learning about it should build respect and safe distance, never encourage approaching or handling.
species.identification: Often glossy black locally, with a broad head and an expandable hood. A snake does not need to raise its hood to be dangerous.
species.diet: Small animals, including rats and toads.
species.activity: Often diurnal, though an encounter is possible at other times.
species.behaviour: May raise the forebody, spread the hood and hiss when threatened. It can also spray venom defensively toward an attacker’s eyes.
species.reproduction: An egg-laying snake. Do not disturb hidden snakes, egg sites or shelter; young snakes must also be left alone.
species.singapore: NParks describes it as common in scrub and suburban habitats. Its secretive nature means encounter frequency and national threat status are different measures.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of small vertebrates in terrestrial food webs.
species.pressures: Killing through fear and conflict with people can harm native snakes.
species.watch: Back away and keep others and pets away. Never try to catch it; seek urgent medical help for a bite or venom exposure.

species.name: Estuarine crocodile
species.habitat: Estuaries, mangroves and former prawn ponds
species.fact: It often basks by day and hunts mainly at night.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2021
species.summary: A large native reptile of estuaries and wetlands. Crocodiles can be difficult to detect in water; viewing must be from designated safe areas.
species.identification: Broad snout, armoured body and a muscular, flattened tail. Only the eyes and nostrils may show above the surface.
species.diet: Fish and other animals; also scavenges.
species.activity: Often basks by day and hunts mainly at night.
species.behaviour: Spends time concealed in water or vegetation. Adults may use freshwater as well as saline habitats despite the name ‘saltwater crocodile’.
species.reproduction: The female lays eggs in a vegetation nest and guards it. A concealed nest area must never be approached.
species.singapore: Recorded from northern wetlands and estuaries, including Sungei Buloh. Records are not an invitation to approach water edges outside permitted areas.
species.ecologicalRole: A large wetland predator and scavenger.
species.pressures: Loss of estuarine habitat and conflict with people. Keeping safe separation protects visitors and wildlife.
species.watch: Follow park warnings and stay on designated paths. Keep well away from water edges, do not feed, and alert park staff to unsafe encounters.

funFacts.title: Not just salt water
funFacts.text: Despite one of its names, it also uses freshwater habitats.

funFacts.text: The female builds a vegetation nest and guards the eggs.

species.name: Four-lined tree frog
species.habitat: Trees and shrubs near breeding water
species.rarity: Common in suburban and disturbed habitats
species.fact: Its eggs begin life inside foam above water; the tadpoles later drop into the water.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A climbing frog of trees, shrubs and gardens. It uses vegetation for hunting and puts its eggs in foam above water rather than laying an exposed mass in a pond.
species.identification: Slender limbs, a pointed snout and expanded toe pads. Four dark back stripes are common, but some individuals are spotted or less clearly marked.
species.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates.
species.activity: Nocturnal.
species.behaviour: Climbs vegetation with its toe pads. Calling can reveal animals that blend into leaves and bark.
species.reproduction: Builds a foam nest over water. After hatching, tadpoles drop into the water and continue development there.
species.singapore: A common native frog of suburban and rural greenery, as well as disturbed forest. It is nationally Least Concern in RDB3.
species.ecologicalRole: An insect predator above ground, with an aquatic tadpole stage linking land and water.
species.pressures: Loss of vegetation and breeding water, disturbance and chemical pollution can reduce suitable habitat.
species.watch: Do not peel open foam nests, collect tadpoles or handle the frogs. Watch from the path.

funFacts.title: A foamy nursery
funFacts.text: Its eggs begin life inside foam above water; the tadpoles later drop into the water.

species.name: Great-billed heron
species.habitat: Coastal shallows, mangroves and islands
species.rarity: Uncommon resident restricted to coastal habitat
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · assessed 2024
species.fact: This heron reaches roughly 1.15 metres in length—a striking contrast with Singapore's tiny kingfishers.
species.globalAssessmentNote: Assessment date and category verified through the IUCN SSC Heron Specialist Group’s Red List table (version 2024-2).
species.summary: A very large coastal heron with an imposing bill. Singapore's population has a Critically Endangered national assessment even though the species has a much wider international range.
species.identification: An adult is mostly dusky grey, with a long neck and unusually heavy, dark pointed bill. Breeding birds develop elongated plumes. Young birds are warmer brown and more streaked. Bird Society of Singapore gives a length of about 114–115 cm.
species.diet: Fish, crustaceans and other aquatic invertebrates.
species.activity: Can be watched feeding at the shoreline by day. The sources used here do not establish an exclusively daytime activity cycle.
species.behaviour: Usually feeds alone, waiting at the water's edge or moving slowly through the shallows before striking at prey.
species.reproduction: NParks describes nesting in isolated mangrove stands. Protecting suitable nesting trees matters; this guide withholds precise breeding locations and gives no unverified local clutch size.
species.singapore: Occurs in coastal settings, including mangroves, estuaries and offshore islands. Its association with specialised coastal habitat makes everyday inland sightings unlikely; a record at one shoreline is not a population estimate.
species.ecologicalRole: Its prey connects intertidal and shallow-water animals to the coastal bird food web.
species.pressures: NParks identifies loss or disturbance of suitable coastal feeding and nesting areas as conservation concerns. Old population estimates in the legacy profile are not presented as current counts.
species.watch: Use coastal hides and public paths. Stay off restricted islands and mangrove nesting areas. Give a feeding bird space instead of following it along the waterline.

funFacts.title: A metre of heron
funFacts.text: This heron reaches roughly 1.15 metres in length—a striking contrast with Singapore's tiny kingfishers.

funFacts.title: Wait, step, strike
funFacts.text: It hunts either by standing still at the edge or by taking slow steps through shallow water.

species.name: Greater mousedeer
species.habitat: Forest understorey
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.
species.summary: A small hoofed forest browser with a rounded body and very slender legs. Its rediscovery on Pulau Ubin shows why an animal missing from casual sightings is not necessarily gone.
species.identification: Reddish-brown fur, pale underparts and contrasting throat markings. More robust than the lesser mousedeer; useful photographs show the neck and chest, not just apparent size. It has no antlers.
species.diet: Fallen fruit, tender leaves and other low-growing plant material.
species.activity: Mostly nocturnal; usually feeds quietly on the forest floor.
species.behaviour: Typically encountered alone while browsing or resting under cover. A published Singapore survey also recorded more than one animal together, so solitary does not mean never seen with another.
species.reproduction: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
species.singapore: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
species.ecologicalRole: A forest-floor plant consumer and part of the food web linking vegetation to predators.
species.pressures: Habitat disturbance and fragmentation can affect its restricted local habitat. Hunting is a pressure across its wider range. Protecting forest cover and limiting disturbance support its persistence.
species.watch: Keep to permitted paths, observe quietly and never feed or pursue it. Leave dense undergrowth undisturbed and do not share exact resting locations.

species.name: Green turtle
species.habitat: Shallow coastal water, reefs and seagrass beds
species.fact: Paddle-shaped limbs power long-distance swimming.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2025
species.summary: A marine turtle that uses tropical and subtropical seas. Adults often graze shallow feeding grounds, while nesting requires accessible sandy beaches.
species.identification: An oval shell with non-overlapping scutes, paddle-like flippers and one pair of scales between the eyes. The shell is usually brownish, not bright green.
species.diet: Adults mainly eat seagrasses and algae; diet changes with life stage.
species.activity: Lives at sea and surfaces for air; nesting is mainly nocturnal.
species.behaviour: Moves between feeding grounds and nesting areas. Its strong front flippers provide propulsion in the water.
species.reproduction: Females dig nests in sandy beaches and bury their eggs. Hatchlings face a separate early life at sea without parental care.
species.singapore: Recorded in the Singapore Straits. Protecting coastal feeding habitat and nesting beaches supports turtles moving through the wider region.
species.ecologicalRole: An important grazer in some seagrass and algal habitats.
species.pressures: Fishing gear, marine pollution, coastal habitat loss and disturbance of nesting beaches.
species.watch: Do not block a turtle’s route or use bright lights around nests. Observe from a distance and report nesting to NParks.

funFacts.title: Green, but not its shell
funFacts.text: Its common name refers to greenish body fat, rather than a green shell.

species.name: Grey heron
species.habitat: River edges, ponds, marshes, mangroves and mudflats
species.summary: A large wading bird that links inland water habitats with the coast. Singapore has both resident and visiting grey herons.
species.identification: Grey and white plumage, long legs, a long neck and a yellowish pointed bill. Adults have a dark stripe extending behind the eye.
species.diet: Fish and other small animals captured near water.
species.activity: Can feed during daylight or at night, depending on conditions.
species.behaviour: Often waits motionless before striking at prey. It usually draws its neck back during flight.
species.reproduction: Builds stick nests, often in colonies. Adults incubate eggs and feed dependent chicks. Do not approach nesting trees or infer local nesting dates from overseas accounts.
species.singapore: Recorded at Sungei Buloh, Kranji and other wetlands. Freshwater margins, mangroves and coastal feeding areas all support it.
species.ecologicalRole: Transfers energy from aquatic prey into the wider wetland food web.
species.pressures: Wetland loss, polluted water and disturbance at feeding or nesting sites can reduce habitat quality. Common sightings are not a population census.
species.watch: Stay on paths and use binoculars. Do not enter colonies, feed birds or approach nests for photographs.
species.fact: A flying heron usually folds its neck back.

funFacts.title: A folded flight posture
funFacts.text: Herons usually fly with the neck pulled back, unlike the extended-neck posture of storks.

funFacts.title: Residents and visitors
funFacts.text: Singapore's grey herons include both resident and migratory birds.

species.name: Hawksbill turtle
species.habitat: Shallow reefs and sandy nesting beaches
species.fact: Its narrow beak helps it reach food such as sponges in reef crevices.
species.rarity: Nesting records do not establish abundance
species.globalStatus: Critically Endangered · 2008
species.summary: A sea turtle associated with tropical reefs. Its narrow, hooked beak reaches into crevices, while adult females depend on suitable beaches to lay eggs.
species.identification: A pointed beak and overlapping shell scutes distinguish typical hawksbills from green turtles. Keep a distance; do not handle a turtle to inspect its shell.
species.diet: Often sponges, with other reef animals also eaten.
species.activity: Marine; females come ashore to nest, usually at night.
species.behaviour: Forages around reef habitat and returns to the surface to breathe. It cannot stay underwater indefinitely.
species.reproduction: Females bury eggs in sand. Hatchlings move toward the sea; people and artificial light can disrupt this vulnerable journey.
species.singapore: Recorded in local waters and nesting on Singapore shores. A nesting record is not a reliable count of the local population.
species.ecologicalRole: A reef consumer, especially of sponges, within marine food webs.
species.pressures: Fishing-gear entanglement, loss or disturbance of beaches, pollution and the international tortoiseshell trade.
species.watch: Keep lights and flash off near nesting turtles. Do not touch adults, eggs or hatchlings; follow NParks’ reporting guidance.

funFacts.text: The shell’s overlapping scutes are a useful hawksbill identification feature.

funFacts.text: Its narrow beak helps reach food tucked into reef crevices.

species.name: Horsfield’s flying squirrel
species.habitat: Forest canopy
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.
species.summary: A nocturnal squirrel that glides between trees on a membrane joining its limbs. Its quiet life above the ground makes it much less conspicuous than the daytime squirrels in parks.
species.identification: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
species.diet: Mainly fruit, with insects also listed in the NParks species account.
species.activity: Active at night; rests in a tree cavity by day.
species.behaviour: Climbs using sharp claws and spreads its membrane to glide. It depends on trees for feeding, shelter and travel. Detailed social behaviour remains poorly studied.
species.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, but the reviewed species account does not establish its mating system, breeding season or litter size. Values from larger flying squirrels are not substituted.
species.singapore: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
species.ecologicalRole: A canopy fruit consumer that also eats small invertebrates. Its precise contribution to seed dispersal in Singapore has not been quantified in the reviewed sources.
species.pressures: Loss of forest and suitable cavity-bearing trees removes shelter and foraging areas. Maintaining connected wooded habitat is important for a species that travels between trees.
species.watch: Observe from permitted routes and avoid flash, sustained spotlighting or disturbance of tree holes. Never lure an animal with food or enter closed areas to seek it.

funFacts.text: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.

species.name: House crow
species.habitat: Urban areas, parks and coastal greenery
species.fact: The house crow is not entirely black: look for its greyer neck and chest.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2018
species.summary: An adaptable crow commonly seen around Singapore’s built areas. It originated in the Indian subcontinent and is an introduced resident here.
species.identification: A black head and wings contrast with a greyer neck and breast. The grey collar is a better starting clue than simply calling any black bird a crow.
species.diet: A wide range of food, including invertebrates, fruit, carrion and accessible food waste.
species.activity: Diurnal.
species.behaviour: Forages opportunistically and can gather around reliable food. Breeding adults may defend the area around their nest or young.
species.reproduction: An egg-laying bird that builds a nest and raises chicks. Defensive swooping can be associated with breeding and does not mean the bird is hunting people.
species.singapore: Common in urban environments and also uses coastal and mangrove settings. It is listed as introduced and nationally Not Applicable.
species.ecologicalRole: A scavenger and omnivore, with possible effects on other birds’ eggs and young.
species.pressures: Food waste and close nesting beside people can lead to conflict.
species.watch: Avoid a defended nesting area and do not feed. Report persistent attacks through the current AVS guidance page.

species.name: Indo-Pacific humpback dolphin
species.habitat: Shallow coastal seas and estuaries
species.rarity: Infrequently seen locally; sightings do not establish population size
species.sourceName: Ocean Park Conservation Foundation Hong Kong
species.summary: A coastal dolphin recorded in Singapore waters. Its common pink-dolphin name does not mean every individual is pink.
species.identification: A long narrow beak and a dorsal fin on a raised back area. Colour varies with age and region; grey markings may remain on pale adults.
species.diet: Small fish captured in coastal waters.
species.activity: Surfaces regularly to breathe between dives; Singapore-specific daily activity patterns are not established here.
species.behaviour: A social, fully aquatic mammal. Surface behaviour can include leaps and raising the head above water.
species.reproduction: Females give birth to calves. Hong Kong research reports a pregnancy of about eleven months. Its seasonal calving pattern must not be treated as a Singapore breeding calendar.
species.singapore: NParks includes this dolphin in Singapore's marine mammal list. Its St John's Island trail factsheet documents sightings around the southern islands. This is wild occurrence, not a captive attraction record.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of coastal fish and part of the marine food web.
species.pressures: Fishing gear, vessel strikes, pollution and coastal habitat disturbance are recognised threats across its range.
species.watch: Do not follow, encircle or feed dolphins. Give them space to travel. Report strandings through local wildlife authorities.
species.fact: Colour changes with age and differs between regions.

funFacts.text: Dolphin colour varies with age and location; some pale adults retain grey spots.

species.name: Javan myna
species.habitat: Lawns, streets, parks and other urban spaces
species.fact: A dark myna reveals bold white wing patches when it takes flight.
species.globalStatus: Vulnerable · 2020
species.summary: A very familiar urban bird in Singapore, introduced through human activity. Its success around people does not make it a native species.
species.identification: Dark grey-black plumage, yellow bill and legs, pale yellow eyes and a short forehead crest. White wing patches show clearly in flight.
species.diet: An adaptable omnivore eating insects, fruit and other available food.
species.activity: Diurnal; gathers at evening roosts.
species.behaviour: Forages on lawns, pavements and in trees. Many individuals can roost together in the same tree.
species.reproduction: Nests in cavities, including suitable openings in buildings. Urban structures can provide many possible nest sites.
species.singapore: Widespread and commonly seen near people. Its national assessment is Not Applicable because it is introduced.
species.ecologicalRole: An urban omnivore that also competes for food and nesting cavities.
species.pressures: Abundant food waste supports concentrations near homes. National non-native status is separate from its conservation position in its native range.
species.watch: Dispose of food properly and do not feed. Leave active nests and roosting birds undisturbed.

species.name: Lesser dog-faced fruit bat
species.habitat: Trees and roosts in urban and forest habitats
species.rarity: Common; hard to identify in flight
species.fact: A fruit bat uses powered flight; the colugo moves by gliding instead.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A small fruit bat that can live in gardens and other urban greenery. Bats are mammals with true powered flight; this species searches for plant food after dark.
species.identification: Brown fur, large eyes, a dog-like muzzle and pale edges along the ears and wing bones. A fast silhouette alone is not enough for species identification.
species.diet: Fruit and nectar.
species.activity: Nocturnal.
species.behaviour: Roosts in small groups in trees, beneath leaves and sometimes buildings. Fruit-bearing plants provide feeding stops across its range.
species.reproduction: Usually bears one pup at a time. Like other mammals, the mother feeds her young with milk.
species.singapore: NParks describes it as widespread and common, including in urban areas. Being hard to identify in flight is different from being nationally rare.
species.ecologicalRole: Helps spread seeds from fruit and can visit flowers for nectar.
species.pressures: Loss of roosts and fruiting vegetation can remove shelter and food.
species.watch: Do not handle a bat or disturb a roost. Observe from a distance and seek professional help for an injured animal.

species.name: Lesser mousedeer
species.habitat: Dense mature forest and its undergrowth
species.rarity: Elusive and restricted to suitable forest
species.fact: Males have extended canine teeth; neither sex grows antlers.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A tiny hoofed forest mammal with a delicate build. It belongs to the chevrotain family, rather than being a mouse or a miniature member of the true deer family.
species.identification: Very slender legs, an arched back, a small pointed face and pale throat markings. It has no antlers.
species.diet: Fallen fruit, young leaves and other forest plant material.
species.activity: Secretive; often concealed in dense undergrowth.
species.behaviour: Moves cautiously through leaf litter. Males have elongated upper canine teeth rather than antlers.
species.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, which are nursed by the mother. Breeding dates are not inferred from isolated local sightings.
species.singapore: Largely associated with mature, dense forest in the Central Nature Reserves. Restricted habitat and quiet behaviour make it difficult to observe.
species.ecologicalRole: A small terrestrial herbivore in the forest-floor food web.
species.pressures: Loss and fragmentation of mature forest reduce suitable cover and feeding habitat.
species.watch: Remain on trails and let it disappear into cover. Do not pursue it for a closer photograph.

species.name: Little egret
species.habitat: Rivers, canals, ponds and coastal wetlands
species.rarity: Common migrant; abundance varies with season and site
species.summary: A small white heron that feeds in shallow water. It uses both urban waterways and natural coastal wetlands.
species.identification: White plumage, a slender dark bill, dark legs and yellow feet in typical adults. Young birds can have greener legs.
species.diet: Small fish, crustaceans and insects. Fish and insects are prey here, not added catalogue groups.
species.activity: Often seen feeding in daylight; feeding opportunities depend on water levels.
species.behaviour: May disturb the water with its feet to reveal prey. It can feed with other egrets.
species.reproduction: Builds nests and lays eggs, often in colonies with other waterbirds. Both parents contribute to care. These species-level notes do not claim a local breeding colony.
species.singapore: A familiar migrant at Sungei Buloh and other wetlands, including pond and canal edges. NParks records it throughout the year, with higher numbers commonly between November and January.
species.ecologicalRole: A shallow-water predator that connects small aquatic animals to the wetland food web.
species.pressures: Wetland disturbance and loss can remove feeding and resting places. A locally common visitor still depends on suitable habitat elsewhere along its migration route.
species.watch: Watch from paths or hides. Avoid making birds fly away from feeding or resting areas, and never feed them.
species.fact: Its yellow feet can stir hidden prey from shallow water.

funFacts.text: A little egret can use its feet to stir prey from the water before striking.

species.name: Long-tailed macaque
species.habitat: Forest edges, mangroves and parks
species.fact: Its tail can rival the combined length of its head and body.
species.globalStatus: Endangered · 2025
species.summary: Singapore’s familiar forest-edge monkey is a social, adaptable native primate. Food left accessible by people can draw groups into close contact with visitors and homes.
species.identification: Brown-grey coat, relatively pale underside and a tail that can be as long as the head and body together. It differs from the dark, pale-banded langur.
species.diet: Fruit and other plant food, plus insects and other small animals.
species.activity: Mainly diurnal.
species.behaviour: Lives in groups organised around related females. It forages both in trees and on the ground and uses calls, expressions and grooming socially.
species.reproduction: Usually gives birth to one infant. Mothers carry and nurse young, which remain within the social group as they grow.
species.singapore: Commonly encountered in and around forest reserves and some parkland. Feeding changes natural foraging behaviour and increases conflict.
species.ecologicalRole: An omnivore and fruit consumer in forest food webs.
species.pressures: Food-conditioned behaviour, unsafe interactions and habitat fragmentation can create local problems, even for a nationally Least Concern species.
species.watch: Keep food out of sight, secure bags and give the group space. Do not stare, feed, tease or try to touch a monkey.

funFacts.title: A long balancing act
funFacts.text: Its tail can rival the combined length of its head and body.

funFacts.title: Family connections
funFacts.text: Groups are organised around female family lines.

species.name: Mainland leopard cat
species.habitat: Forest, scrubland and plantations
species.fact: This nocturnal hunter is mainly terrestrial but also climbs easily.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2022
species.summary: A small wild cat with a spotted coat, rather than a miniature leopard. This quiet hunter uses forest, scrub and plantations and can be difficult to distinguish in a brief night-time glimpse.
species.identification: Yellowish or reddish-buff fur with dark spots; rounded ears have pale spots on their black backs. It has a short muzzle and rounded head.
species.diet: Small vertebrates such as rodents, frogs, lizards and birds.
species.activity: Mostly nocturnal.
species.behaviour: Often solitary. Hunts mainly on the ground but is an able climber. A single photograph may not be enough to rule out a domestic cat.
species.reproduction: Females raise dependent kittens in sheltered dens. The regional literature describes small litters; this is not a Singapore breeding forecast.
species.singapore: NParks documents records from wooded areas on the mainland and offshore islands. These scattered records do not imply that all such places hold resident populations.
species.ecologicalRole: A small predator within the forest food web, including predators of rodents.
species.pressures: Habitat loss and possible illegal trapping are identified in the NParks profile.
species.watch: Do not pursue it or disclose a den location. Report suspected trapping to the relevant wildlife authority.

funFacts.text: The back of each rounded ear carries a pale spot against black fur.

species.name: Malayan horned frog
species.habitat: Mature forest streams
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Its angular outline and brown colouring help a motionless frog disappear among fallen leaves.
species.summary: A leaf-shaped ambush hunter from Singapore's mature forests. Its camouflage is so effective that a call may reveal a frog that the eye has missed.
species.identification: Broad angular head, pointed eyelid projections and a leaf-like snout and brown body. Females are larger than males. Projection length varies, so it should not be the only identification feature.
species.diet: Animal prey on the forest floor, including invertebrates and small vertebrates such as other frogs or lizards.
species.activity: Secretive; calls can be heard around dusk and were recorded during late-afternoon breeding observations in Singapore.
species.behaviour: Remains still in leaf litter and ambushes passing prey. Local researchers have often detected it by its distinctive loud call near streams.
species.reproduction: Breeds in forest streams. A Singapore field study recorded mating and a cluster of gelatinous eggs attached beneath partly submerged bark; larvae develop in water.
species.singapore: Associated with patches of mature forest in the Central Nature Reserves. It is nationally Critically Endangered in RDB3; this guide avoids breeding-site directions.
species.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator that connects leaf-litter prey with larger forest predators; its aquatic young also depend on stream habitat.
species.pressures: Loss or damage to moist forest and stream habitat is a concern, alongside collection for the pet trade across its range.
species.watch: Listen from open trails during permitted hours. Do not use call playback, move leaf litter, enter breeding streams or handle frogs and eggs.

funFacts.text: Its angular outline and brown colouring help a motionless frog disappear among fallen leaves.

species.name: Malayan porcupine
species.habitat: Mature forest
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.
species.summary: A large ground-dwelling rodent with striking defensive quills. Camera traps helped establish that this secretive native mammal still survived in Singapore after decades with few reports.
species.identification: A blunt muzzle, stout body, short legs and a short tail. The longest back quills are strongly patterned in black and white. It is a porcupine, not a hedgehog.
species.diet: Fruit, roots and stems, gathered while foraging on the ground.
species.activity: Nocturnal; normally shelters in burrows during daylight.
species.behaviour: Digs burrows and travels on land. A threatened animal can raise its quills, rattle its tail and back towards a threat; leave it room to retreat.
species.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
species.singapore: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
species.ecologicalRole: Its plant feeding links roots, stems and fallen fruit to the forest food web; burrowing also disturbs small patches of soil.
species.pressures: Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Hunting for meat and trade in body parts are documented regional pressures; the reviewed sources do not provide a current Singapore hunting rate.
species.watch: Keep a generous distance and never block its path or approach a burrow. Do not attempt to handle an animal or remove its quills.

funFacts.text: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.

funFacts.text: Hollow quills on the short tail make a rattling sound when shaken.

species.name: Malayan water monitor
species.habitat: Mangroves, ponds, reservoirs and parks
species.fact: Young water monitors have brighter spotted patterns than many large adults.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2021
species.summary: A large lizard commonly seen beside Singapore’s water. It is an able swimmer, but can also walk on land and climb trees.
species.identification: Long neck, forked tongue, sturdy claws and a powerful tail. Young animals show yellowish spots and bands that can fade as they mature.
species.diet: Small animals, including fish, and carrion.
species.activity: Diurnal.
species.behaviour: Searches for food near water and may bask on banks. Its forked tongue samples chemical cues in the environment.
species.reproduction: Females lay eggs in sheltered sites on land, including suitable decaying wood or soil. Young monitors are independent after hatching.
species.singapore: Widespread, including mangroves, ponds and parks. A large water monitor is a lizard, not a juvenile crocodile.
species.ecologicalRole: Both predator and scavenger in waterside food webs.
species.pressures: Unsafe encounters, road crossings and disturbance can affect animals living beside people.
species.watch: Give it space and a route away. Do not feed, touch or provoke it; a defensive bite can injure.

species.name: Oriental pied hornbill
species.habitat: Parks and wooded areas with fruiting trees
species.fact: A nesting female stays inside a mostly sealed tree cavity while the male brings food.
species.rarity: Recovered; often visible at suitable sites
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2020
species.summary: A conspicuous black-and-white bird with a pale bill and a raised casque. Its return to Singapore is a conservation story linked to suitable habitat and nesting places.
species.identification: Large pale bill, casque above the bill, black wings and upperparts, and a white belly. Look at several features rather than comparing it with a toucan.
species.diet: Mainly fruit, supplemented by small animals.
species.activity: Diurnal; calls and travels through wooded areas.
species.behaviour: Visits fruiting trees and may travel in pairs or groups. Tree cavities are essential for its unusual nesting routine.
species.reproduction: The female and chicks stay in a mostly sealed cavity. The male brings food through a narrow opening.
species.singapore: Now found in suitable parks and wooded areas, including Pulau Ubin. Recovery does not make every site suitable for nesting.
species.ecologicalRole: Fruit consumption can move seeds between patches of vegetation.
species.pressures: Loss of large cavity-bearing trees and disturbance at nests. Nest boxes have supported local conservation efforts.
species.watch: Leave fruit for wildlife. Do not feed, crowd or approach a nesting cavity.

funFacts.title: Room service in a tree
funFacts.text: The male delivers meals through the small entrance of the sealed nest.

funFacts.title: A bill with a helmet
funFacts.text: The raised structure on top of the bill is called a casque.

species.name: Plantain squirrel
species.habitat: Trees in forests, parks and gardens
species.fact: Listen for loud chirps and chatter while squirrels move among branches.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A familiar squirrel of Singapore’s trees and gardens. It spends daylight hours searching for food and moving quickly between trunks and branches.
species.identification: A bushy tail and a pale stripe above a darker stripe on each flank are useful clues. Check side markings, rather than relying on coat colour alone.
species.diet: Fruit, seeds and other plant food, with some animal food.
species.activity: Diurnal.
species.behaviour: Uses claws to climb and makes quick leaps between branches. Chirps and chatter are part of its communication.
species.reproduction: Young are born in a sheltered nest and depend on their mother. Leave leafy nests undisturbed even when they appear empty.
species.singapore: NParks describes it as the most common squirrel in local urban parks and gardens. It also uses forest and other wooded habitats.
species.ecologicalRole: A seed and fruit consumer within tree-based food webs.
species.pressures: Loss of tree connections and feeding by people can affect normal movement and foraging.
species.watch: Enjoy it from the path. Do not bait it for a photograph or offer snacks.

species.name: Purple heron
species.habitat: Vegetated wetlands and marshes
species.rarity: Resident; easily hidden in dense wetland plants
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · assessed 2019
species.fact: Its elongated toes help it place careful steps on marsh plants and floating vegetation.
species.globalAssessmentNote: Assessment date and category verified through the IUCN SSC Heron Specialist Group’s Red List table (version 2024-2).
species.summary: A slender heron adapted to wetland vegetation. Its chestnut neck, dark lines and patient stillness make it less obvious among stems than its name might suggest.
species.identification: Adults have a long chestnut neck marked with dark stripes, a dark cap, greyish upperparts and a narrow pointed bill. Young birds are browner and lack the adult's strong neck markings. It is around 78–90 cm long.
species.diet: Fish are important prey, alongside frogs, aquatic invertebrates and other small animals; diet varies with habitat and prey availability.
species.activity: Often forages around morning and evening, but can also feed in daylight. Local observation times do not establish a fixed island-wide schedule.
species.behaviour: Waits among dense plants or moves slowly through shallow water to catch prey. Long toes help it negotiate emergent and floating vegetation.
species.reproduction: Builds a platform of reeds or sticks in wetland vegetation; trees and thickets can also be used. Both parents incubate and feed the young. Regional breeding seasons and clutch sizes vary, so none is presented here as a Singapore norm.
species.singapore: A resident species recorded in freshwater wetlands and coastal vegetation. NParks lists the Central Catchment, Sungei Buloh and Pulau Ubin. It can be familiar at suitable wetlands while remaining nationally Endangered.
species.ecologicalRole: A wetland predator linking small aquatic animals to the bird food web.
species.pressures: The Heron Specialist Group identifies wetland alteration and disturbance as pressures across its range. Retaining suitable vegetated feeding and nesting habitat is a relevant local priority; no current Singapore decline rate is asserted.
species.watch: Use hides and stay on public paths. Do not enter reedbeds, cut vegetation or flush a hidden bird into view. Keep nesting habitat undisturbed.

species.name: Raffles's banded langur
species.habitat: Mature forest canopy in the Central Catchment
species.fact: This arboreal leaf-eater digests vegetation in a multi-chambered stomach.
species.globalStatus: Critically Endangered · 2022
species.summary: One of Singapore’s rarest primates, this leaf-eating monkey depends on mature forest. It is different from the more familiar long-tailed macaque seen at forest edges.
species.identification: Mostly dark fur, a long tail and contrasting pale areas on the underside and inner limbs. Observe the whole pattern and body shape from a distance.
species.diet: Leaves, unripe fruit and other plant material.
species.activity: Mainly active during daylight in the canopy.
species.behaviour: Lives in social groups and spends much of its time in trees. Its specialised stomach supports digestion of leafy food.
species.reproduction: Infants have a much paler coat than adults and depend on maternal care. Their colouring changes as they grow.
species.singapore: The local population is very small and concentrated in the Central Catchment. The species also occurs in southern Peninsular Malaysia.
species.ecologicalRole: A forest canopy herbivore, linked to the diversity of its food plants.
species.pressures: Small population size and fragmented forest make protection of habitat and connectivity important.
species.watch: Use open trails and binoculars. Do not follow a group off-trail, play calls or share sensitive locations.

funFacts.text: Young langurs start much paler than the dark adults and change colour as they grow.

species.name: Red-cheeked flying squirrel
species.habitat: Mature forest canopy
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
species.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
species.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
species.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
species.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
species.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
species.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
species.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
species.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
species.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
species.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

species.name: Red junglefowl
species.habitat: Forest edges, scrub and wooded parks
species.rarity: Often seen; domestic hybrids complicate identification
species.fact: Despite feeding on the ground, junglefowl roost in trees.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2024
species.summary: The wild relative of domestic chickens. Singapore also has free-ranging domestic and hybrid chickens, so every rooster in a park must not be labelled a pure red junglefowl.
species.identification: Males have orange-red neck feathers, dark glossy tails and a red comb. Females are mottled brown. Domestic ancestry cannot be ruled out from one visible trait.
species.diet: Seeds, roots and small invertebrates found on the ground.
species.activity: Diurnal; roosts in trees at night.
species.behaviour: Scratches and pecks through ground cover. Groups have social relationships, with males displaying and crowing.
species.reproduction: Females lay eggs in a ground nest and care for chicks. The young can follow the mother and feed themselves soon after hatching.
species.singapore: Native wild birds and admixed free-ranging birds occur locally. The national Near Threatened assessment applies to the wild species, not all domestic chickens.
species.ecologicalRole: A ground-foraging omnivore that eats seeds and small animals.
species.pressures: Hybridisation with domestic chickens, trapping and loss of suitable habitat.
species.watch: Do not feed or chase. Give hens with chicks room to move and leave ground nests alone.

species.name: Reticulated python
species.habitat: Forest, waterways and urban cover
species.fact: ‘Reticulated’ describes the net-like pattern running along its body.
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2018
species.summary: A large native snake with a network-like pattern. It is non-venomous but powerful, and should always be observed without handling or cornering it.
species.identification: Tan or yellow-brown ground colour crossed by dark geometric lines and pale side patches. Its shape and pattern differ from a uniformly dark cobra.
species.diet: Mammals, including rodents; larger individuals can take larger prey.
species.activity: Often nocturnal or hidden during daylight.
species.behaviour: Ambushes prey, constricts it and swallows it whole. It is mainly terrestrial but can climb well.
species.reproduction: Lays eggs; the female coils around the clutch during incubation. Eggs and resting snakes must not be moved by visitors.
species.singapore: A native resident using natural and urban habitats. A drain or green corridor can provide cover, so sightings are not limited to forests.
species.ecologicalRole: A predator of rodents and other mammals.
species.pressures: Road collisions, persecution and conflict in built environments.
species.watch: Keep people and pets away and allow an escape route. Contact a wildlife professional if it is trapped or inside a building.

species.name: Small-toothed palm civet
species.habitat: Forest canopy
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: A published Singapore record describes two civets resting against each other in the canopy; the observers could not confirm their relationship.
species.summary: A canopy-dwelling civet that is much less often seen than Singapore's familiar Sumatran palm civet. Published observations of adults and apparent young show how much remains to learn about its forest life.
species.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
species.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.
species.activity: Nocturnal and strongly arboreal; often rests high in vegetation.
species.behaviour: Often described as solitary. Singapore observers have also recorded pairs resting close together, although their ages and relationship could not always be confirmed.
species.reproduction: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
species.singapore: Associated with the central nature reserves. A 2023 NUS biodiversity record documents observations in secondary forest during 2022–2023. Exact resting trees are omitted from this guide.
species.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
species.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
species.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.

funFacts.title: A treetop cuddle
funFacts.text: A published Singapore record describes two civets resting against each other in the canopy; the observers could not confirm their relationship.

funFacts.title: Carnivore, fruit included
funFacts.text: Belonging to the order Carnivora does not mean an all-meat menu: fruit is an important food for this civet.

species.name: Smooth-coated otter
species.habitat: Mangroves, reservoirs, ponds and urban canals
species.fact: Social family groups use both natural and highly urban waterways.
species.rarity: Regular at some waterways; nationally threatened
species.globalStatus: Vulnerable · 2021
species.summary: A social water-loving mammal that has returned to Singapore’s waterways. Family groups can live close to people, but they still need space to feed, rest and raise pups.
species.identification: A long brown body, short smooth fur and a paler throat and underside. It is larger than the Asian small-clawed otter; do not identify the species from size alone.
species.diet: Mainly fish, with other aquatic prey.
species.activity: Active on land and in water; sightings vary with the group and site.
species.behaviour: Travels and feeds in family groups. Groups use scent and calls and may compete with other families over territory.
species.reproduction: Pups are raised in sheltered dens, with adults attending them. Keep away from resting and den areas even if no adult is visible.
species.singapore: Uses mangroves, reservoirs, ponds and urban canals. Frequent sightings at one waterway do not change its national Endangered status.
species.ecologicalRole: An aquatic predator connecting waterways and adjacent land habitats.
species.pressures: Road crossings, disturbance and unsafe encounters can affect urban families. Connected, usable waterways remain important.
species.watch: Keep your distance and do not block the route between the group and water. Keep dogs leashed and never feed otters.

funFacts.title: Family travellers
funFacts.text: Several generations can share a family group and move along waterways together.

funFacts.title: A city comeback
funFacts.text: Singapore now has breeding otter families using urban as well as natural waterways.

species.name: Spiny hill turtle
species.habitat: Mature forest
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.fact: Its dramatic juvenile shell edges become much less spiky as the turtle grows.
species.summary: A forest-floor turtle with an especially striking shell when young. Singapore's remaining mature forests shelter this locally Endangered reptile.
species.identification: Brown shell with a raised middle ridge and jagged rear edge; dark head and limbs, with reddish marks beside the head. Young turtles have much sharper shell-edge projections than adults.
species.diet: An omnivore. Regional research records fruit and other plant material, some animal food and mushrooms; the proportions in Singapore have not been measured here.
species.activity: NParks describes mainly nocturnal activity; this is not a rule that excludes daytime encounters.
species.behaviour: Adults spend much of their time on land. Younger turtles use water more extensively, so forest-floor and stream habitats both matter.
species.reproduction: Lays eggs. Breeding has been achieved in conservation collections; no Singapore nesting month or clutch-size claim is made here.
species.singapore: Native populations are associated with the Central Nature Reserves. The national assessment is Endangered in RDB3; encounter locations and resting sites are not mapped here.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes material from several parts of the forest food web. Mushroom eating is documented, but effective fungal-spore dispersal by this species remains a research question.
species.pressures: Forest degradation and collection for trade threaten it. Protecting habitat and preventing collection are central conservation needs.
species.watch: Keep to open paths, leave it where it is and avoid handling or flash. Do not disclose a precise location or collect an animal for a pet.

funFacts.title: Growing out of the spikes
funFacts.text: Its dramatic juvenile shell edges become much less spiky as the turtle grows.

funFacts.title: Mushroom on the menu
funFacts.text: A study published in 2026 describes a wild spiny turtle eating a mushroom in Borneo, an observation made in 2020.

species.name: Straw-headed bulbul
species.habitat: Dense foliage near rivers and forest edges
species.fact: Its loud song has made it a target of the illegal songbird trade.
species.globalStatus: Critically Endangered · 2018
species.summary: A large songbird whose voice often gives it away before its body appears. Singapore is important to its survival, while capture for the songbird trade has damaged populations elsewhere.
species.identification: A straw-coloured crown, dark facial stripes and pale streaks on the breast. It is larger than many familiar urban bulbuls.
species.diet: Fruit, berries and insects.
species.activity: Diurnal; often heard from dense vegetation.
species.behaviour: Forages in thick foliage near water and forest edges. Its loud, bubbling song is a useful clue, but listening must not become playback or disturbance.
species.reproduction: An egg-laying bird whose nesting cover needs protection. Do not seek nests or publish nest locations; local timing is not predicted by this guide.
species.singapore: Found in suitable wooded habitats, including Pulau Ubin. Local occurrence and its global Critically Endangered label refer to different geographic scales.
species.ecologicalRole: A fruit-eater and insect predator within wooded habitats.
species.pressures: Illegal capture for the songbird trade and habitat loss. Singapore’s species action plan includes habitat work and protection against poaching.
species.watch: Listen quietly from paths. Never play calls to draw it out, set up bait or publicise a nest.

species.name: Sumatran palm civet
species.habitat: Woodland, gardens and some urban areas
species.rarity: Widespread but mostly hidden by day
species.fact: Seeds from fruit meals can be spread in a civet’s droppings.
species.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
species.summary: A nocturnal fruit-eater and small-animal hunter, often known locally as the common palm civet. It can move through both trees and settled areas in search of food.
species.identification: A long body and tail, pointed muzzle and dark facial markings. It is a civet, not a domestic cat despite the nickname ‘toddy cat’.
species.diet: Fruit, berries and small animals, including insects.
species.activity: Nocturnal; usually rests out of sight by day.
species.behaviour: Often forages alone, using branches and the ground. Adaptability allows it to visit gardens and buildings beside green spaces.
species.reproduction: Females give birth to dependent young in sheltered places. Avoid disturbing roof spaces or tree hollows occupied by a family.
species.singapore: A native resident of wooded areas and some neighbourhoods. The name Sumatran palm civet follows NParks’ current species table.
species.ecologicalRole: Passes seeds from eaten fruit, helping seed dispersal.
species.pressures: Road crossings, loss of shelter and conflict around homes. Wildlife-friendly coexistence is preferable to feeding or trapping.
species.watch: Secure food waste and allow it to leave. If young are present, seek AVS advice before closing an access hole.

funFacts.title: An after-dark gardener
funFacts.text: Seeds from fruit meals can be spread in a civet’s droppings.

funFacts.title: A misleading nickname
funFacts.text: A ‘toddy cat’ belongs to the civet family, not the cat family.

species.name: Sunda colugo
species.habitat: Tall forest, nearby parkland and plantations
species.fact: Its broad patagium supports controlled glides between trees.
species.rarity: Restricted range; rarely seen, but locally common at some sites
species.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2008
species.summary: A tree specialist that travels on a sheet of skin. Colugos glide between trunks instead of flapping wings, and spend much of the day pressed quietly against bark.
species.identification: Look for mottled grey-brown fur, large eyes, curved claws and a broad membrane joining the limbs and tail. The folded membrane can be hard to see on a resting animal.
species.diet: Young leaves, shoots, flowers and fruit.
species.activity: Mainly nocturnal; rests on trees by day.
species.behaviour: Climbs to gain height before a glide. Camouflage and stillness help it stay unnoticed. It is neither a bat nor a true lemur.
species.reproduction: Usually one young is born. The infant clings to its mother; she can fold her gliding membrane around it for support and warmth.
species.singapore: Associated with tall forest in the Central Nature Reserves and connected wooded spaces. A quiet, hidden animal may be present even when visitors do not notice it.
species.ecologicalRole: A canopy herbivore that links plant growth to the forest food web.
species.pressures: Loss of connected tree cover reduces feeding areas and routes through the canopy.
species.watch: Stay on open trails. Use binoculars and avoid flash or shining a light into its eyes.

funFacts.title: A blanket that glides
funFacts.text: A mother can fold her gliding membrane into a pouch around her young.

funFacts.title: Flying in name only
funFacts.text: The ‘flying lemur’ is neither a lemur nor a powered flier.
